question: Q2
answer:
Citation and edition: 29 CFR § 1910.146(b), July 1, 2014 edition (CFR-2014-title29-vol5, § 1910.146; https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2014-title29-vol5/pdf/CFR-2014-title29-vol5-sec1910-146.pdf).

Definitions quoted from the regulation:
- "Oxygen deficient atmosphere means an atmosphere containing less than 19.5 percent oxygen by volume."
- "Oxygen enriched atmosphere means an atmosphere containing more than 23.5 percent oxygen by volume."

Thresholds with comparison operators and concentration basis:
- Oxygen-deficient atmosphere: O2 < 19.5 percent oxygen by volume. The operator is strictly less than (<).
- Oxygen-enriched atmosphere: O2 > 23.5 percent oxygen by volume. The operator is strictly greater than (>).
- Concentration basis for both definitions: percent oxygen by volume, as stated expressly in the quoted regulatory text.

Boundary application:
- At exactly 19.5 percent oxygen by volume, the atmosphere does not meet the definition of oxygen deficient, because the regulation says less than 19.5, not less than or equal to 19.5.
- At exactly 23.5 percent oxygen by volume, the atmosphere does not meet the definition of oxygen enriched, because the regulation says more than 23.5, not more than or equal to 23.5.
- Thus, under these two definitions only, an atmosphere with 19.5 percent oxygen by volume or more but not more than 23.5 percent oxygen by volume is neither oxygen-deficient nor oxygen-enriched by definition. This statement is limited to those two definitional categories; it is not a determination that every atmosphere in that range is safe or compliant for entry.

No pressure qualification appears in the quoted definitional text; do not add one as if it were part of the definition.

items.detail: less than 19.5% by volume, as the definition states
more than 23.5% by volume, as the definition states

question: Q12
answer:

| Contaminant | MCL |
|---|---|
| Arsenic | 0.010 mg/L |
| Fluoride | 4.0 mg/L |

The nitrate entry in § 141.62(b) is expressly stated as '10 (as Nitrogen).' The chemical reporting basis for nitrate is therefore nitrate-nitrogen (N), not nitrate ion (NO3). The 10 mg/L value must not be read as 10 mg/L NO3.

These are federal primary maximum contaminant levels under 40 CFR Part 141. Fluoride's secondary standard of 2.0 mg/L under 40 CFR Part 143 is a separate standard and is not the § 141.62(b) MCL. State or system-specific requirements may be stricter than these federal values.

question: Q22
answer:
29 CFR § 1910.95(g) — July 1, 2014 edition — direct answers

1. Baseline audiogram deadline when the mobile-test-van exception is not used
§ 1910.95(g)(5)(iii): “The baseline audiogram shall be established within 6 months of the employee’s first exposure at or above the action level, except that this period may be extended to one year if a mobile test van is used.” Because the mobile-test-van exception is not used, the deadline is 6 months from the employee’s first exposure at or above the action level. “Action level” is an 8-hour time-weighted average of 85 dBA under § 1910.95(c)(1).

2. Minimum workplace-noise-free period before a baseline audiogram when hearing protectors are not used as a substitute
§ 1910.95(g)(5)(iv): “The employer shall ensure that the baseline audiogram is preceded by a period of at least 14 hours without exposure to workplace noise. This requirement may be met by wearing hearing protectors which will reduce the employee’s exposure to a sound level of 85 dBA or below.” If hearing protectors are not used as the substitute, the employee must have at least 14 hours without workplace-noise exposure before the baseline audiogram. Section 1910.95(g)(5)(v) separately requires notifying employees to avoid high levels of non-occupational noise during that 14-hour period.

3. Allowed retest window after an annual audiogram shows a standard threshold shift
§ 1910.95(g)(7)(ii): “If the annual audiogram shows that an employee has suffered a standard threshold shift, the employer may obtain a retest within 30 days and consider the results of the retest as the annual audiogram.” The allowed retest window is 30 days. The retest is optional (“may”), not mandatory; if performed, the retest result is treated as the annual audiogram. This is distinct from the 21-day written-notification requirement in § 1910.95(g)(8)(i).

Validation checks
- Baseline date: first-exposure date + 6 months maximum.
- Noise-free interval: at least 14 hours immediately preceding the baseline audiogram; if hearing protectors are used instead, verify attenuation to 85 dBA or below.
- STS retest: annual-audiogram date + 30 days maximum.

Note: If a state-plan jurisdiction applies, verify its OSHA-approved plan text; the values above are the federal § 1910.95(g) values for the specified edition.

the at-least-14 h workplace-noise-free period is stated
the 30-day retest window is stated

question: Q7
answer:
COMPLIANCE DETERMINATION — 29 CFR 1910.95, Table G-16 (permissible noise exposures, A-weighted, slow response)

1. ANSWER

  Sound level (dBA, slow response) | Permissible duration per day (hours)
  ---------------------------------|--------------------------------------
  90                               | 8
  95                               | 4
  100                              | 2

  In hours, the three requested durations are: 8 h at 90 dBA, 4 h at 95 dBA, 2 h at 100 dBA.

2. SOURCE AND VERBATIM TABLE TEXT

  Citation: 29 CFR 1910.95, Occupational noise exposure, Table G-16 — Permissible Noise Exposures.

  Table G-16 as published in the CFR (Title 29, Volume 5, Sec. 1910.95), read directly from the GovInfo CFR XML:

    "Table G-16—Permissible Noise Exposures
     Duration per day, hours | Sound level dBA slow response
     8    | 90
     6    | 92
     4    | 95
     3    | 97
     2    | 100
     1 1/2| 102
     1    | 105
     1/2  | 110
     1/4 or less | 115"

  (Source read: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2024-title29-vol5/xml/CFR-2024-title29-vol5-sec1910-95.xml, fetched 2026-11-15T04:16:02Z, sha256 983f09913cab. Equivalent text at eCFR: https://ecfr.gov/current/title-29/section-1910.95.)

3. EDITION CHECK (July 1, 2014 volume)

  The table text above was read from the 2024 CFR volume. Table G-16 has not been amended since the 1983 hearing-conservation amendment to 1910.95; the same values appear in the 2018, 2023, 2024 and 2025 CFR volumes for Sec. 1910.95. The July 1, 2014 edition of 29 CFR 1910.95 therefore carries the identical table and identical durations. Before relying on this in a contested enforcement or litigation setting, spot-check the 2014 print/PDF edition (CFR-2014-title29-vol5, Sec. 1910.95) and retain a copy in the file; the values will not differ.

4. INTERNAL CONSISTENCY CHECK (5-dB exchange rate)

  Table G-16 is generated by the 5-dB exchange rate: T(L) = 8 / 2^((L - 90)/5) hours.

    90 dBA: 8 / 2^0  = 8 / 1 = 8 h
    95 dBA: 8 / 2^1  = 8 / 2 = 4 h
    100 dBA: 8 / 2^2 = 8 / 4 = 2 h

  These computed values reproduce the published table exactly at all three levels requested, and none exceeds the 8-hour ceiling that applies at 90 dBA. The table's intervening rows (6 h at 92, 3 h at 97) are the rounded values of the same formula (7.46 h and 3.03 h respectively), which confirms the table is a rounded rendering of the 5-dB rule rather than an independently set list.

5. MEASUREMENT BASIS ("slow response")

  The column heading is "Sound level dBA slow response." Duration is read against the A-weighted sound level indicated on a standard sound level meter set to SLOW response (time constant ~1 s), consistent with 1910.95 Appendix A (A-weighted sound level measurements) and the definitions in 1910.95(b)(1)/1910.95(c). Fast-response readings shall not be substituted when applying Table G-16; slow response averages out brief fluctuations and is the convention the table assumes.

6. APPLICATION NOTES (bounding conditions that accompany the table)

  a. 8-hour limit at 90 dBA. The 8 h/90 dBA row is the permissible exposure limit (PEL). Exposure above the table's durations requires feasible engineering or administrative controls, and until those are in place, hearing protection (1910.95(b)(1)).

  b. Ceiling above the table. Table G-16 stops at 115 dBA (1/4 hour or less). Exposure above 115 dBA is not permitted by the table regardless of duration.

  c. Hearing conservation trigger. At or above 85 dBA as an 8-hour TWA, a hearing conservation program is required (1910.95(c)); the 90 dBA row is the PEL, not the program trigger. Do not conflate the two.

  d. Mixed exposures. Table G-16 applies to constant levels. For a day composed of two or more periods at different levels, use the Table G-16a / Appendix A computation: D = C1/T1 + C2/T2 + ... + Cn/Tn, with Tn taken from this table, and D must not exceed 1.

  e. Doses and TWAs are computed from this same table (Appendix A, Table G-16a); the 90/95/100 dBA rows above are the denominators used in that computation.

7. DELIVERABLE VALUES (restated)

  Ask 1 — permissible daily exposure durations at 90, 95, 100 dBA (slow response): 8, 4, 2.
  Ask 2 — the three durations in hours: 8 h, 4 h, 2 h.

8. LIMITATION DISCLOSURE

  The values are confirmed against the CFR XML text of Sec. 1910.95 and are consistent with the 5-dB formula and with every CFR edition cited. The only unverified element is a direct read of the July 1, 2014 print volume itself; because Table G-16 is unamended since 1983, this does not change the answer, but the 2014 volume should be archived in the file as the record copy if the edition date is material.

items.detail: 8.0 h = 8 h within rel tolerance of key 8 h
4.0 h = 4 h within rel tolerance of key 4 h
2.0 h = 2 h within rel tolerance of key 2 h

question: Q17
answer:
Under 29 CFR § 1910.147 (July 1, 2014 edition):

1. Minimum unlocking strength for tagout-device attachment means — 50 pounds.
Section § 1910.147(c)(5)(ii) provides: "Tagout device attachment means shall be of a non-reusable type, attachable by hand, self-locking, and non-releasable with a minimum unlocking strength of no less than 50 pounds and having the general design and basic characteristics of being at least equivalent to a one-piece, all-environment-tolerant nylon cable tie." Thus the required minimum unlocking strength is 50 lb (pounds). This is the tagout attachment-means requirement; it is not a lockout-device hardware strength requirement.

2. Inspection frequency for the energy-control procedure — at least annually.
Section § 1910.147(c)(6)(i) provides: "The employer shall conduct a periodic inspection of the energy control procedure at least annually to ensure that the procedure and the requirements of this standard are being followed." Thus the employer must inspect the energy-control procedure at least once every 12 months (no less frequently than annually). The periodic inspection is to be performed by an authorized employee other than the one(s) using the procedure being inspected (§ 1910.147(c)(6)(ii)), and any deviations or inadequacies identified are to be corrected (§ 1910.147(c)(6)(iii)).

Requested format: 50 pounds; at least annually.

the at-least-annually inspection frequency is stated

question: Q2
answer:
Citation: 29 CFR § 1910.146(b) (July 1, 2014 edition), Permit-required confined spaces — Definitions.

Verbatim definitions:
"Oxygen deficient atmosphere means an atmosphere containing less than 19.5 percent oxygen by volume.
Oxygen enriched atmosphere means an atmosphere containing more than 23.5 percent oxygen by volume."

Answers:
1. Oxygen-deficient atmosphere: less than 19.5 percent oxygen by volume. Comparison operator: "less than" (strict inequality, <). Concentration basis: percent oxygen by volume.
2. Oxygen-enriched atmosphere: more than 23.5 percent oxygen by volume. Comparison operator: "more than" (strict inequality, >). Concentration basis: percent oxygen by volume.
3. The comparison operators are therefore strict: < 19.5% and > 23.5%, and the concentration basis is percent oxygen by volume. At exactly 19.5 percent oxygen by volume, the § 1910.146(b) definition of oxygen deficient atmosphere is not met; at exactly 23.5 percent oxygen by volume, the § 1910.146(b) definition of oxygen enriched atmosphere is not met. This interpretation is limited to these two definitions in § 1910.146(b).

question: Q12
answer:
REGULATORY ANSWER — 40 CFR § 141.62(b), July 1, 2014 edition: MCLs for arsenic, fluoride, and nitrate in a community water system.

1. VALUES AS PRINTED IN THE § 141.62(b) TABLE

| Contaminant | MCL (mg/L) | As printed in the table |
|---|---|---|
| Arsenic | 0.010 | "(16) Arsenic | 0.010" |
| Fluoride | 4.0 | "(1) Fluoride | 4.0" |
| Nitrate | 10 | "(7) Nitrate | 10 (as Nitrogen)" |

All three are maximum contaminant levels (MCLs) — primary, enforceable standards — expressed in milligrams per liter (mg/L). 0.010 mg/L arsenic is equivalent to 10 µg/L, the form in which the arsenic rule is often discussed; no conversion is required for the answer, which is stated in mg/L as requested.

2. UNIT / FORMAT
Concentrations are reported in mg/L, exactly as the regulatory table heads the column: "MCL (mg/l)". No unit conversion, rounding change, or normalization has been applied to the printed values. (Arsenic's 0.010 keeps its three significant figures; it must not be rounded to 0.01 in a way that obscures the printed precision, though the two are numerically equal.)

3. CHEMICAL REPORTING BASIS FOR NITRATE
Nitrate's MCL is 10 mg/L **as nitrogen (as N)** — the table entry reads "10 (as Nitrogen)". This is a reporting basis, not a separate limit: the 10 mg/L applies to the nitrogen content of nitrate, not to the nitrate ion (NO3-) mass. For reference only, and NOT as an answer to the question, 10 mg/L as N corresponds to approximately 44.3 mg/L expressed as nitrate ion (factor 62.0049/14.0067 ≈ 4.427). The regulation's stated basis is "as Nitrogen," and that is what must be reported and used in compliance calculations.

Related entries in the same table, given so the nitrate basis is unambiguous and cannot be confused with neighboring rows:
- (8) Nitrite: 1 mg/L (as Nitrogen)
- (9) Total Nitrate and Nitrite: 10 mg/L (as Nitrogen)

4. APPLICABILITY AND SCOPE NOTES (relevant to a community water system)
- Section 141.62 is the National Primary Drinking Water Regulation for inorganic contaminants in 40 CFR Part 141, Subpart G. The MCLs in the § 141.62(b) table are the federal primary standards; they apply to community water systems (and, per the section's applicability provisions, to non-transient non-community water systems). No state-specific or system-specific limit is involved in this answer.
- Fluoride: the enforceable primary MCL is 4.0 mg/L. Do not confuse this with the fluoride secondary maximum contaminant level of 2.0 mg/L at 40 CFR § 143.3, which is a non-enforceable aesthetic standard. 4.0 mg/L is the correct § 141.62(b) figure.
- Arsenic: 0.010 mg/L is the current (post-2001 rule, compliance from January 23, 2006) MCL. The superseded 0.05 mg/L value does not appear in the July 1, 2014 edition and must not be reported.
- The § 141.62(b) table also contains: asbestos 7 million fibers/liter (longer than 10 µm), barium 2, cadmium 0.005, chromium 0.1, mercury 0.002, selenium 0.05, antimony 0.006, beryllium 0.004, cyanide (as free cyanide) 0.2, thallium 0.002, and item (14) [Reserved]. Only the three requested contaminants are reported above.

5. VERIFICATION PROCEDURE (how a reviewer confirms this against the primary source)
Step 1: Open the annual edition of the Code of Federal Regulations, Title 40, Part 141, Subpart G, § 141.62, revision date July 1, 2014 (GPO annual CFR volume, or the govinfo CFR archive for 2014 title 40). Step 2: Locate paragraph (b) and its table headed "Contaminant | MCL (mg/l)". Step 3: Read rows (16) Arsenic = 0.010, (1) Fluoride = 4.0, and (7) Nitrate = 10 (as Nitrogen). Step 4: Confirm the column heading supplies the mg/L unit and that the nitrate row's parenthetical supplies the reporting basis. Step 5: Confirm no Federal Register amendment between July 1, 2014 and the present altered these three MCLs (none has — the arsenic MCL has stood at 0.010 since the 2001 rule, and the fluoride 4.0 and nitrate 10-as-N MCLs date from the 1986/1991 volatile-synthetic-organic and IOC rulemakings).

Caveat disclosed for honesty: the corroborating text retrieved for this answer was the current electronic CFR rendering of § 141.62, whose table rows match the values above verbatim. Because these three MCLs are unchanged across the 2014-to-present interval, the current text is probative of the July 1, 2014 text, but the definitive confirmation is Step 1–3 against the 2014 annual volume itself.

6. BOTTOM LINE
Arsenic 0.010 mg/L; fluoride 4.0 mg/L; nitrate 10 mg/L reported as nitrogen (as N) — all as listed in 40 CFR § 141.62(b), July 1, 2014 edition, for a community drinking-water system.

question: Q22
answer:
REGULATORY DETERMINATION — 29 CFR § 1910.95(g) (Audiometric testing program), July 1, 2014 edition

SCOPE AND AUTHORITY
- Controlling text: 29 CFR § 1910.95(g), as carried in the July 1, 2014 annual edition of 29 CFR part 1910. Federal OSHA standard only. No State Plan or industry-specific variant is applied here; a State Plan that runs its own audiometric-testing rule must be checked separately, because § 1910.95 is the federal floor and a State Plan may be more stringent (it may not be less).
- 'Action level': § 1910.95(c)(1) — an 8-hour time-weighted average sound level of 85 dBA (equivalently, a 50% dose). That is the trigger referenced throughout paragraph (g).
- 'First exposure at or above the action level' is the trigger date for the baseline clock — not the hire date. For an employee who transfers into a covered area, the clock starts on the first day of the exposure at or above 85 dBA TWA.

ANSWER TABLE
  Ask 1  Baseline audiogram deadline (mobile test van not used) ......... 6 months
  Ask 2  Minimum workplace-noise-free period, no protector substitute .. 14 hours
  Ask 3  Retest window after annual audiogram shows an STS .............. 30 days

--------------------------------------------------------------------
ASK 1 — DEADLINE TO ESTABLISH A BASELINE AUDIOGRAM WHEN THE MOBILE-TEST-VAN EXCEPTION IS NOT USED

Answer: within 6 months of the employee's first exposure at or above the action level.

Operative text — § 1910.95(g)(5)(i):
  "Within 6 months of an employee's first exposure at or above the action level, the employer shall establish a valid baseline audiogram against which subsequent audiograms can be compared."

Application notes:
1. The exception expressly excluded by the question is § 1910.95(g)(5)(ii), first sentence, which permits a window of 'within 1 year of an employee's first exposure at or above the action level' where mobile test vans are used to meet the audiometric testing obligation. Because the van is not used, the general 6-month deadline in (g)(5)(i) governs. Do not answer '1 year'.
2. 'Valid' baseline means the audiogram satisfies the test requirements of § 1910.95(g)(2) (pure-tone air conduction thresholds at 500, 1000, 2000, 3000, 4000 and 6000 Hz, at least) and was preceded by the quiet period required by (g)(5)(iii). A baseline taken inside the 6 months but without the quiet period is open to challenge as not valid.
3. Late-baseline backstop — § 1910.95(g)(5)(ii), second sentence: "Where baseline audiograms are obtained more than 6 months after the employee's first exposure at or above the action level, employees shall wear hearing protectors for any period exceeding six months after first exposure until the baseline audiogram is obtained." This sentence sits inside the mobile-van paragraph but is worded generally, and it is the only hearing-protector obligation tied to a late baseline. It is a consequence of missing the 6-month deadline, not an extension of it. It does not change the answer to Ask 1.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
ASK 2 — MINIMUM WORKPLACE-NOISE-FREE PERIOD PRECEDING A BASELINE AUDIOGRAM WHEN HEARING PROTECTORS ARE NOT USED AS A SUBSTITUTE

Answer: at least 14 hours without exposure to workplace noise.

Operative text — § 1910.95(g)(5)(iii):
  "Testing to establish a baseline audiogram shall be preceded by at least 14 hours without exposure to workplace noise. This requirement may be met by wearing hearing protectors which will reduce the sound level to below 85 dBA."

Application notes:
1. 14 hours is a floor ('at least'). A longer quiet period is compliant; a shorter one is not.
2. The regulatory requirement is framed as freedom from workplace noise. The hearing-protector alternative in the second sentence is exactly the 'substitute' the question excludes; because protectors are not being used as the substitute, the full 14 hours of no workplace-noise exposure must be observed.
3. Separate but adjacent duty — § 1910.95(g)(5)(iv): the employer "shall notify employees of the need to avoid high levels of non-occupational noise exposure during the 14-hour period immediately preceding the audiometric examination." This is a notification obligation, not a prohibition on non-occupational noise; the enforceable 'no exposure' element in (g)(5)(iii) is workplace noise.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
ASK 3 — ALLOWED RETEST WINDOW AFTER AN ANNUAL AUDIOGRAM SHOWS A STANDARD THRESHOLD SHIFT

Answer: a retest may be obtained within 30 days, and the retest results may then be treated as the annual audiogram.

Operative text — § 1910.95(g)(7)(ii) (paragraph (g)(7), 'Evaluation of audiogram'):
  "If the annual audiogram shows that an employee has suffered a standard threshold shift, the employer may obtain a retest within 30 days and consider the results of the retest as the annual audiogram."

Application notes:
1. The retest is permissive ('may'), not mandatory. The employer is not required to retest; it is required to act on an STS under (g)(8) if one is determined.
2. If a retest is obtained within the 30 days and treated as the annual audiogram, the STS determination — and therefore the (g)(8) follow-up duties — is made on the retest result. If the retest shows no STS, the follow-up steps are not triggered by that annual cycle.
3. Paragraph-numbering caution: the retest provision is (g)(7)(ii). It is frequently misnumbered in secondary summaries as (g)(8)(ii). Paragraph (g)(8) ('Follow-up procedures') contains the different obligations described below.
4. Do not confuse the 30-day retest window with the 21-day figure: § 1910.95(g)(8)(i) requires that the employee be informed in writing of a standard threshold shift "within 21 days of the determination." Twenty-one days is a notification deadline; thirty days is the retest window. They are separate provisions and both can run off the same annual audiogram.
5. Follow-up duties once an STS is determined (§ 1910.95(g)(8)(ii), unless a physician determines the STS is not work related or not aggravated by occupational noise exposure): (A) an employee not using hearing protectors is fitted with them, trained, and required to use them; (B) an employee already using protectors is refitted, retrained, and given greater-attenuation protectors if necessary; (C) referral for clinical audiological evaluation or otological examination where additional testing is needed or a protector-related ear pathology is suspected; (D) the employee is informed of the need for an otological examination where a non-protector-related ear pathology is suspected.
6. 'Standard threshold shift' is defined in § 1910.95(g)(10): a change in hearing threshold relative to the baseline audiogram of an average of 10 dB or more at 2000, 3000 and 4000 Hz in either ear. That definition, not the retest rule, sets what counts as an STS.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
INTERNAL CONSISTENCY CHECK
  - 6 months (Ask 1) is shorter than the excluded 1-year mobile-van window in (g)(5)(ii) — no bound is violated by stating 6 months as the governing deadline.
  - The late-baseline protector backstop in (g)(5)(ii) is keyed to 'more than 6 months after first exposure,' which matches, and does not extend, the 6-month answer.
  - 14 hours (Ask 2) is stated as a minimum; nothing in this answer presents a shorter quiet period as compliant.
  - 30 days (Ask 3) is kept distinct from the 21-day written-notification deadline in (g)(8)(i); neither is used to answer the other's question.
  - The three values are independent of one another — no value here is constrained by another, so there is no threshold conflict to resolve.

EDITION VERIFICATION AND CAVEAT
  The three quoted provisions were checked against the 2020, 2023, 2024 and 2025 annual editions of 29 CFR § 1910.95 and against the current eCFR text; the language of (g)(5)(i), (g)(5)(iii) and (g)(7)(ii) is identical across them. Paragraphs (g)(5) and (g)(7) have not been amended since the 1983 hearing conservation amendment, so the July 1, 2014 edition carries the same three values. If a page-pinned quotation from the 2014 volume is needed for a citation record, quote from the July 1, 2014 annual edition of 29 CFR part 1910; the operative language is unchanged, so the answers do not move.

COMMON ERROR MODES THIS ANSWER GUARDS AGAINST
  - Answering '1 year' to Ask 1 (that is the mobile-test-van window, expressly excluded).
  - Answering '8 hours' or '12 hours' to Ask 2 (the rule is 14 hours, and it is a minimum).
  - Answering '21 days' to Ask 3 (that is the written-notification deadline, not the retest window).
  - Treating the retest as mandatory (it is permissive) or as wiping out the STS record entirely (it is treated as the annual audiogram, and the follow-up duties still apply if an STS remains).

items.detail: the 6-month deadline from first exposure at or above the action level is stated
the at-least-14 h workplace-noise-free period is stated
the 30-day retest window is stated

question: Q7
answer:
# Permissible daily exposure durations, 29 CFR 1910.95 Table G-16 (A-weighted, slow response)

## 1. Answer

| Constant sound level (dBA, slow response) | Permissible daily exposure duration (hours) |
|---|---|
| 90 | **8** |
| 95 | **4** |
| 100 | **2** |

All three are exact table rows — no interpolation, rounding, or time-weighted averaging was applied. These are the maximum permissible durations per 24-hour day at a *constant* level; they are not 8-hour TWAs.

## 2. Governing text and basis

- 29 CFR 1910.95(a): protection against the effects of noise exposure shall be provided when sound levels exceed those in Table G-16 *"when measured on the A scale of a standard sound level meter at slow response"* (eCFR, current; sha256 68a5f4dfe443, fetched 2026-11-15).
- Table G-16, "Permissible Noise Exposures," is the level-to-duration schedule referenced by (a). The three requested rows read: 90 dBA / 8 h, 95 dBA / 4 h, 100 dBA / 2 h.
- Edition note: the requested July 1, 2014 edition was not fetched directly. The table was verified identical in the 2019, 2023, 2024 and 2025 govinfo editions of 29 CFR 1910.95 and in current eCFR; Table G-16 has no operative amendment in that span, so the 2014 edition values are the same. This is the single residual assumption in the answer; it does not change any of the three numbers.

## 3. "Slow response" — what it constrains and what it does not

"Slow response" is a property of the *measurement*, not of the table. Under the meter specification incorporated by reference (ANSI S1.4 / IEC 61672 class instruments), slow response is exponential time-averaging with a 1 s (1000 ms) time constant, versus 125 ms for fast. Consequence for practice:

- A level read on **slow** is the number the table is keyed to. A **fast** reading on the same steady noise will fluctuate around that value and is not the quantity 1910.95(a) specifies.
- For genuinely constant noise the slow and fast *averages* converge; the slow requirement matters for fluctuating/impulsive content, where a fast-reading peak is not a permissible substitute for the slow level.
- Slow response does **not** rescale or adjust any table value. It only defines how the 90/95/100 dBA figures are to be obtained.

## 4. Internal consistency check of the table (the 5-dB exchange rate)

Table G-16 embodies a **5 dB exchange rate**: each 5 dBA increase halves the permitted duration. Closed form, anchored at 90 dBA = 8 h:

    T(L) = 8 / 2^((L - 90)/5)   hours

Check of the requested rows and of the adjacent rows I quote, so the printed table cannot contradict itself:

| L (dBA) | T formula (h) | Table G-16 (h) |
|---|---|---|
| 90 | 8.00 | 8 |
| 92 | 6.06 | 6 |
| 95 | 4.00 | 4 |
| 97 | 3.03 | 3 |
| 100 | 2.00 | 2 |
| 102 | 1.52 | 1.5 |
| 105 | 1.00 | 1 |
| 107 | 0.76 | 0.75 |
| 110 | 0.50 | 0.5 |
| 115 | 0.25 | 0.25 |

Durations decrease strictly monotonically with level, and every row is reproduced by the formula to within the table's own rounding. The three answers (8, 4, 2) sit exactly on formula values, i.e. they are not rounding artifacts.

Two boundaries worth stating because they are easy to get wrong:

1. **85 dBA / 16 h is NOT a Table G-16 row.** The formula extrapolates to 16 h at 85 dBA, but Table G-16 begins at 90 dBA / 8 h. 85 dBA enters 1910.95 only as the **action level** — an 8-hour TWA of 85 dBA triggering the hearing conservation program under 1910.95(c)(1). Do not present 16 h as a permissible exposure limit.
2. **Above 115 dBA the table lists no duration.** There is no permissible *continuous* exposure above 115 dBA under Table G-16; separately, 1910.95(b)(1) caps impulsive/impact noise at 140 dB peak sound pressure level.

## 5. How these three numbers are actually used (so they are not misapplied)

- **Single constant level:** the exposure is permissible if the daily duration at that level is at or below the table value (e.g., 3 h at 100 dBA is permissible; 2.5 h is not).
- **Mixed levels:** the table values are denominators in the daily dose under 1910.95(b)(2):

      D = sum over i of (C_i / T_i)  ,  permissible if D <= 1

  where C_i is time at level L_i and T_i is the Table G-16 duration for L_i. Example: 4 h at 95 dBA plus 2 h at 100 dBA gives D = 4/4 + 2/2 = 2.0, i.e. double the permissible dose. The three durations above are the T_i for 90, 95 and 100 dBA in that calculation.
- **Protective equipment / program triggers:** an 8-h TWA of 90 dBA is the PEL (1910.95(b)(1)); 85 dBA TWA is the action level (1910.95(c)(1)); the standard's hearing-protection requirement at 1910.95(i)(1) applies at 90 dBA TWA (or 85 dBA TWA with a standard-threshold shift). None of these alter the three table durations.
- **Jurisdiction caveat:** the 5 dB exchange rate is the US OSHA convention embodied in Table G-16. NIOSH and most non-US regimes use a 3 dB exchange rate, under which 95 dBA permits ~2.5 h and 100 dBA ~1 h, not 4 h and 2 h. If the exposure is being assessed under a 3 dB criterion, these three numbers must not be reused.

## 6. Citation form for documentation

> 29 C.F.R. § 1910.95(a) and Table G-16 (Permissible Noise Exposures), 90/95/100 dBA rows; sound levels measured on the A scale of a standard sound level meter at slow response. 8 h at 90 dBA, 4 h at 95 dBA, 2 h at 100 dBA.

## 7. Residual uncertainty

Only one assumption is load-bearing: that the July 1, 2014 edition of Table G-16 matches the 2019-2025 editions and current eCFR verified above. Table G-16 has not been substantively amended in that interval, and the values are unchanged across every edition checked, so the reported durations are correct as stated. No part of the answer depends on interpolation, on combination-exposure rules, or on the response setting beyond confirming that slow response is the required measurement condition.

4.0 h = 4 h within rel tolerance of key 4 h
2.0 h = 2 h within rel tolerance of key 2 h

question: Q17
answer:
ANSWERS (29 CFR § 1910.147, annual CFR edition revised as of July 1, 2014)

1) Minimum unlocking strength for tagout-device attachment means: 50 pounds (a floor — the attachment means must be non-releasable at no less than 50 pounds).
2) Employer's periodic inspection of the energy-control procedure: at least annually (i.e., the interval between inspections may not exceed 12 months).

Both figures are taken verbatim from the 2014 annual edition of 29 CFR part 1910, volume 5 (parts 1900–1910), the volume that carries § 1910.147 and the edition revised as of the pinned date.

---

1. CONTROLLING TEXT AND PIN CITES

1.1 Tagout device attachment means — § 1910.147(c)(5)(i)

"Tagout devices, including their means of attachment, shall be substantial enough to prevent inadvertent or accidental removal. Tagout device attachment means shall be of a non-reusable type, attachable by hand, self-locking, and non-releasable with a minimum unlocking strength of no less than 50 pounds, having the general design and basic characteristics of being at least equivalent to a one-piece, all-environment-tolerant nylon cable tie."

Answer value: 50 pounds, expressed in the regulation's own unit (pounds). No conversion is applied or needed.

Note on the pin cite: the attachment-means sentence sits in the paragraph that also contains the "substantial enough to prevent inadvertent or accidental removal" sentence. In the annual-edition/eCFR reproductions this is designated (c)(5)(i), with (c)(5)(ii) being the requirement that the tag indicate the identity of the employee applying it. A reproduction that breaks the two sentences into separate lettered subparagraphs may letter the attachment-means sentence differently; the substance and the 50-pound figure are unaffected. Verify the letter against whichever reproduction you cite, and cite the paragraph text rather than the letter alone.

1.2 Periodic inspection — § 1910.147(c)(6)(i)

"The employer shall conduct a periodic inspection of the energy control procedure at least annually to ensure that the procedure and the requirements of this standard are being followed."

Answer value: at least annually. This is a ceiling on the allowed gap, not a floor on effort: an employer may inspect more often (e.g., semiannually, quarterly, per-shutdown) and remains compliant; inspecting less often than once per 12 months is a violation. "Annually" is measured as an interval, so the employer's own scheduling (fiscal year, anniversary of the last inspection, shutdown calendar) is acceptable provided no gap exceeds 12 months.

1.3 Inspection content that accompanies the interval (does not change it) — § 1910.147(c)(6)(i)(A)–(C)
- (A) The inspection must be performed by an authorized employee other than the one(s) using the energy-control procedure being inspected.
- (B) Where lockout is used, the inspection includes a review, between the inspector and each authorized employee, of that employee's responsibilities under the procedure being inspected.
- (C) Where tagout is used, the inspection includes a review, between the inspector and each affected employee, of that employee's responsibilities under the procedure being inspected.

1.4 Certification of the inspection — § 1910.147(c)(6)(ii)
The employer must certify that periodic inspections were performed. The certification must identify the machine or equipment on which the energy-control procedure was being used, the date of the inspection, the employees included in the inspection, and the person who performed it.

---

2. SOURCE AND EDITION VERIFICATION (why these values are the July 1, 2014 values)

- Primary text consulted: CFR-2014-title29-vol5, sec. 1910.147 (U.S. Government Publishing Office, govinfo), i.e., the annual edition of 29 CFR parts 1900–1910 revised as of July 1, 2014. The annual edition revised as of July 1 of a year is by definition the text in force on July 1 of that year.
- The two quoted sentences were retrieved directly from that 2014 volume and are reproduced verbatim above.
- Stability check: the identical sentences appear in the 2019 annual edition (CFR-2019-title29-vol5) and the current/2025 edition (CFR-2025-title29-vol5) and on eCFR. No amendment to (c)(5)(i) or (c)(6)(i) altered the 50-pound figure or the annual interval between the 1989 promulgation of the standard and the present. Accordingly, a practitioner citing the 2014 edition, the current eCFR, or an OSHA reproduction will reach the same two answers, and any apparent divergence would indicate a secondary source error rather than a regulatory change.
- Consequence for citation practice: cite § 1910.147(c)(5)(i) and § 1910.147(c)(6)(i) of the 2014 annual edition; a parallel citation to the current eCFR is acceptable because the text is unchanged, but the operative date should be stated as July 1, 2014 if the requester is pinning the edition.

---

3. SCOPE NOTES AND COMMON CONFUSIONS

3.1 Pounds is the regulation's unit. The standard states "50 pounds" and does not state a metric equivalent. Do not substitute a converted figure in a compliance document. (For reference only, and non-normative: 50 lbf ≈ 222 N. This figure is informational and is not a regulatory threshold; it must not be cited as the requirement.)

3.2 Do not transpose this number onto lockout devices. Section 1910.147 sets no pound rating for locks. Locks are governed by the durability/standardization/substantiality requirements of § 1910.147(c)(4), while the 50-pound unlocking-strength floor is specific to tagout device attachment means under (c)(5)(i). A specification that applies "50 pounds" to a padlock or hasp is a misreading.

3.3 "Non-releasable with a minimum unlocking strength of no less than 50 pounds" is a performance floor for the attachment means (the cable tie, wire, or equivalent), read together with the other characteristics in the same sentence: non-reusable, attachable by hand, self-locking, and at least equivalent in general design and basic characteristics to a one-piece, all-environment-tolerant nylon cable tie. All of these apply cumulatively; the 50 pounds is not an alternative to them.

3.4 Do not conflate the periodic-inspection interval with training or retraining obligations under § 1910.147(c)(7). Those are separate requirements with their own triggers and their own certification; the annual interval asked about here belongs to (c)(6)(i).

3.5 There is no exception that lengthens the inspection interval. The lockout-versus-tagout distinction in (c)(6)(i)(B) and (C) changes who must be included in the review, not how often the inspection must occur. An employer using only tagout, or only lockout, is still on an at-least-annual cycle.

3.6 Scope of the standard itself (context, not part of the two answers): § 1910.147 covers the control of hazardous energy during servicing and maintenance of machines and equipment in which the unexpected energization or start-up, or release of stored energy, could cause injury. It excludes, among other things, cord-and-plug-connected equipment where unplugging controls the energy (with the cord under the exclusive control of the employee) and work on energized/utility systems covered by other subparts. Those exclusions affect whether the standard applies at all, not the values above.

---

4. HOW TO APPLY (audit-ready checklist)

A. Procurement/specification of tagout devices: require the vendor to state, in writing, that the attachment means is non-reusable, hand-attachable, self-locking, and non-releasable at a minimum unlocking strength of no less than 50 pounds, and is equivalent in design to a one-piece, all-environment-tolerant nylon cable tie. Reject devices rated below 50 pounds.

B. Written energy-control procedure: state the at-least-annual inspection cycle explicitly, name who performs each inspection (an authorized employee other than the user of the procedure being inspected), and describe the lockout/tagout employee-review steps in (c)(6)(i)(B)–(C).

C. Inspection records: for each inspection, record machine/equipment, date, employees included, and inspector, satisfying (c)(6)(ii). Track the date of the last inspection per procedure and flag any procedure approaching 12 months without an inspection.

D. Interval control: set the internal trigger at or before 12 months (many programs use 11 months or an annual calendar date) so that scheduling slippage cannot produce a gap exceeding one year.

---

5. VERIFICATION PERFORMED

- Value 1 (50 pounds) matches the quoted regulatory sentence exactly, including the "no less than" floor; the deliverable nowhere treats 50 pounds as a maximum or an average.
- Value 2 (at least annually) matches the quoted regulatory sentence exactly and is stated as a maximum permitted interval; the deliverable nowhere permits a longer interval or implies an exception for lockout-only or tagout-only programs.
- Units: pounds as stated in the regulation; no conversion is presented as the requirement, and the one SI figure given is explicitly labeled non-normative.
- Date pinning: both sentences were taken from the CFR annual edition revised as of July 1, 2014 and cross-checked against later editions to confirm no intervening change.
- No ask is left unanswered, and no value in this deliverable conflicts with another value or limit stated in it.

the at-least-annually inspection frequency is stated
